title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target.
hints: Think about what you'd need to know about previous numbers as you iterate.
A hash map can store value -> index as you go.
For each number, check if target - num exists in the map already.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i], without using division.
hints: Think about prefix and suffix products.
Compute prefix products left-to-right in one pass.
Then multiply by suffix products right-to-left in a second pass.

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
hints: Water trapped at index i depends on the max height to its left and right.
Try precomputing left-max and right-max arrays.
A two-pointer approach can do this in O(n) with O(1) extra space.

title: Valid Anagram
statement: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise.
hints: Think about character frequency counts.
Sort both strings and compare, or use a frequency map.
Counter/dict comparison is the simplest O(n) approach.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
hints: Think sliding window.
Use a set to track characters currently in the window.
When you hit a duplicate, shrink the window from the left until it's gone.

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together.
hints: Anagrams share the same sorted character sequence.
Use the sorted string (or character count tuple) as a hash map key.
Group all original strings under their canonical key.

title: Invert Binary Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, invert the tree, and return its root.
hints: Think recursively: invert the subtrees first.
At each node, swap the left and right children.
A simple recursive function handles this in a few lines.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST).
hints: A node's value must fall within a valid (low, high) range from its ancestors.
Pass down updated bounds recursively.
In-order traversal of a valid BST should be strictly increasing.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values (left to right, level by level).
hints: BFS using a queue is the natural fit.
Process one full level at a time by tracking the queue size at the start of each level.
Append a new list for each level's values.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
statement: Design an algorithm to serialize and deserialize a binary tree to/from a string.
hints: Pre-order traversal works well for serialization.
Use a marker (e.g. 'null') for missing children.
Deserialize recursively, consuming tokens from the front of the list.

title: Number of Islands
statement: Given an m x n 2D binary grid which represents a map of '1's (land) and '0's (water), return the number of islands.
hints: Think of each land cell as a graph node connected to adjacent land cells.
DFS or BFS from each unvisited '1' to mark its whole island as visited.
Count how many times you start a new traversal.

title: Course Schedule II
statement: Given numCourses and a list of prerequisite pairs, return the ordering of courses you should take to finish all courses, or an empty array if impossible.
hints: Think about representing this as a graph problem.
What traversal handles dependency ordering?
Topological sort via BFS (Kahn's algorithm) or DFS works well.

title: Word Ladder
statement: Given two words and a dictionary, return the length of the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time.
hints: Model each word as a graph node, edges connect words differing by one letter.
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
Generate neighbors by changing each letter position to a-z and checking the dictionary.

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You are climbing a staircase that takes n steps. Each time you can climb 1 or 2 steps. Return the number of distinct ways to climb to the top.
hints: This is just Fibonacci in disguise.
ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
Use two variables to track the last two values instead of recursion.

title: Coin Change
statement: Given coins of different denominations and a total amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount, or -1 if impossible.
hints: Build a dp array where dp[i] = min coins to make amount i.
dp[0] = 0; for each amount, try every coin.
dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1) for each coin <= i.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
hints: dp[i] = length of the LIS ending at index i.
For each i, check all j < i where nums[j] < nums[i].
For O(n log n), maintain a sorted 'tails' array and binary search for insertion point.
